extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (also useful to patent practitioners and applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether claim limitations add 'significantly more' than a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, natural phenomenon) — i.e., whether limitations are more than mere instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, or mere field-of-use linking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether an element is more than mere instructions to apply an exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether an element (or combination of elements) is more than mere instructions to apply an exception (e.g., mere instructions to implement an abstract idea on a computer).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should explain why limitations that are merely instructions to 'apply it' do not meaningfully limit the claim in an eligibility rejection. Examples and case law are used to show when recitations (such as implementing on a generic computer) do not add significantly more (e.g., Alice). For claim limitations that do not amount to more than a recitation of the words 'apply it', examiners should explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim and consult MPEP § 2106.07(a) for formulating rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess if the claim fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished and instead attempts to cover any solution with no description of the mechanism (i.e., result-oriented or functional claiming).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result-oriented claims that lack specifics about how a computer performed modifications or produced results are equivalent to the words 'apply it' and do not provide significantly more (see Electric Power Group; Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One). In contrast, claiming a particular solution or a particular way to achieve an outcome may provide significantly more. Examples of unacceptable/result-oriented recitations include claims that merely describe creating or modifying documents without the specific steps of how the modifications are performed (Intellectual Ventures v. Capital One). Courts have repeatedly found claims ineligible when they are 'so result focused, so functional, as to effectively cover any solution to an identified problem.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the claim uses a computer or machinery only in its ordinary capacity to perform an existing process (e.g., to receive, store, or transmit data), which does not add significantly more to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using generic computer components or claiming improved speed/efficiency solely due to a general-purpose computer does not provide an inventive concept (see Affinity Labs; TLI Communications; Intellectual Ventures I LLC v. Capital One Bank). In contrast, claims that improve computer capabilities or another technology may provide significantly more (see McRO; Enfish). Examples of mere tool use include applying a commonplace business method or algorithm on a general purpose computer (Alice), generating a second menu via generic components (Apple v. Ameranth), or monitoring audit logs on a general-purpose computer where gains are only due to the computer's capabilities (FairWarning). See MPEP § 2106.05(a) and § 2106.05(f) for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: The particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether the claim's applicability is broad across many fields or whether it is confined to a particular, practical application of the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims with broad applicability across many fields may not provide meaningful limitations and can amount to merely adding 'apply it' (see Internet Patents v. Active Network; O’Reilly v. Morse; The Telephone Cases). Limitations that confine an abstract idea to a particular, practical application may amount to significantly more (see BASCOM and Diehr). Courts look for concrete, integrated limitations acting in concert to transform or improve a technical process (Diehr: monitoring, measuring, repetitively calculating, and automatically opening press). Examples of merely generic field limitations include broadly reciting a technological environment without integration (Affinity Labs; Flook). The presence or absence of integration of the limitation into the claim as a whole is a key factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional elements add more than insignificant extra-solution activity (activities incidental to the primary process or product that are merely nominal or tangential additions, including pre- and post-solution activity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extra-solution activity includes pre-solution steps (e.g., gathering data) and post-solution steps (e.g., printing a report) that are incidental. The addition of insignificant extra-solution activity does not amount to an inventive concept (Parker v. Flook; Mayo). Examiners should evaluate each claim on its merits and consider other Step 2B factors (e.g., particular machine, transformation, well-understood routine conventional activity, field of use). Factors to consider when assessing insignificant extra-solution activity: (1) Whether the extra-solution limitation is well known (token/known techniques indicate insignificance; see Bilski; Flook; Intellectual Ventures v. Erie Indem. Co.), (2) Whether the limitation is significant (i.e., imposes meaningful limits on the claim rather than being nominal or tangential; see Ultramercial; Apple v. Ameranth), and (3) Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting (e.g., Mayo; OIP Technologies). The guidance lists many examples of activities courts found insignificant: Mere data gathering (clinical tests to obtain inputs, testing systems for response, presenting offers and gathering statistics, obtaining transaction information, consulting logs, measuring biomarkers), selecting particular data sources/types (limiting database index to XML tags; limiting orders to table-based customers), and insignificant application (cutting hair after determining style; printing/downloading generated menus). Some cases identify insignificant computer implementation as an example (Fort Properties; Bancorp Services). For limitations deemed insignificant extra-solution activity, examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim (see MPEP § 2106.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use and technological environment limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether additional elements do more than generally link the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use; mere field-of-use limitations do not make a claim patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim cannot be made eligible simply by limiting the formula or abstract idea to a particular technological use (Diamond v. Diehr; Parker v. Flook; Bilski). Token or incidental field-of-use limitations (e.g., limiting administration of a drug to a particular patient population; specifying commodity providers/consumers; limiting a formula to a specific type of object) do not add an inventive concept (Mayo; Bilski; Flook). The key distinction is whether the field-of-use limitation is integrated into the claim as a whole and alters how steps are performed (Diehr’s integrated process vs Flook’s non-integrated limitation). Recent cases (Affinity Labs) show that merely confining an abstract idea to a device class (e.g., cellular telephones) is insufficient. Examiners should look for absence/presence of integration and consult examples (Diehr integrated steps vs Flook token field-of-use) to determine whether the limitation adds significantly more.
